title: Syndromic Management of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
sourceOrganization: Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) & WHO
summary: Ethiopian national syndromic flowcharts treat identifiable STI symptom clusters (discharge, ulcers, pelvic pain) on the same day without waiting for lab cultures.
keyPoints: Common syndromic presentations: abnormal vaginal or urethral discharge, burning urination (dysuria), genital ulcers, and pelvic pain.
Asymptomatic Reality: Over 70% of women and up to 50% of men carry chlamydia or gonorrhea with ZERO noticeable symptoms; lack of symptoms does not mean absence of infection or transmission.
Simultaneous Dual Partner Treatment: Both sexual partners MUST be treated at the exact same time; treating only one leads to immediate ping-pong reinfection.
Never Stop Antibiotics Early: Always complete the full prescribed antibiotic regimen even if symptoms vanish within 48 hours to prevent antimicrobial resistance and deep pelvic scarring.
Abstain from sexual intercourse until at least 7 days after both partners complete all prescribed medications.
detailedContent: In resource-limited health facilities, syndromic management groups symptoms into defined clinical syndromes (such as Vaginal Discharge Syndrome or Genital Ulcer Disease).

Health Extension Workers and clinical officers can immediately initiate first-line combination therapy for both Gonorrhea and Chlamydia simultaneously, saving critical time and preventing fallopian tube scarring.
whenToSeeClinician: Visit your Kebele Health Post or Woreda Health Center within 24 to 48 hours if you notice burning urination, discolored discharge, or sores.
ethiopiaContext: Standard of care across all Ethiopian primary healthcare units and youth corners.

title: Simultaneous Dual Partner Treatment for STIs
summary: Both sexual partners must take prescribed STI treatment at the exact same time to prevent ping-pong reinfection.
keyPoints: Treating only one partner leads to immediate ping-pong reinfection upon next intercourse.
Most partners of infected individuals carry the bacterium or virus even without noticeable symptoms.
Ethiopian clinics provide partner notification slips or expedited partner therapy packages.
Refrain from unprotected sex until at least 7 days after completing medication.
detailedContent: Failure to treat sexual partners is the leading cause of recurrent pelvic pain, persistent discharge, and antimicrobial resistance.
Clinicians in Ethiopia are trained to facilitate confidential partner treatment without blame, moralizing, or confrontation.
whenToSeeClinician: Bring your partner or inform your clinician so both of you can receive appropriate prescriptions together.
ethiopiaContext: Free partner counseling and notification support available at public Health Centers and Marie Stopes clinics.

title: Asymptomatic & Silent STIs in Women and Men
sourceOrganization: UNFPA & Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH)
summary: Over 70% of women and up to 50% of men infected with chlamydia or gonorrhea experience zero early physical symptoms.
keyPoints: Absence of symptoms does NOT mean absence of infection or transmission risk.
Untreated silent STIs can quietly ascend into the uterus and fallopian tubes, leading to Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) and ectopic pregnancy.
Routine annual or pre-pregnancy STI screening detects silent infections early.
Syphilis screening with rapid RPR/Treponemal tests is mandatory during early antenatal care (ANC).
detailedContent: Because bacterial pathogens often colonize the cervix without generating painful nerve sensations, women often remain unaware of infection until severe complications emerge.
Dual protection using latex condoms alongside regular checkups is the most reliable defense.
whenToSeeClinician: Request an STI and syphilis screen whenever you have a new partner or during your first antenatal checkup.
ethiopiaContext: Integrated into national antenatal care (ANC) and youth-friendly reproductive health services.

title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) & Cervical Cancer Prevention
sourceOrganization: Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) & GAVI
summary: Draft overview of HPV transmission through genital contact, primary school vaccination programs, and Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) screening.
keyPoints: HPV is the most common viral STI, transmitted through skin-to-skin genital contact.
High-risk HPV strains cause >95% of cervical cancer cases worldwide.
Ethiopia administers the HPV vaccine to 14-year-old schoolgirls nationwide.
Women aged 30 to 49 should undergo routine Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) screening every 3 to 5 years.
detailedContent: Draft clinical notes: HPV vaccination schedule updates and single-dose recommendation protocols currently pending clinical panel review.
VIA and cryotherapy services are offered free of charge in Ethiopian district hospitals.
whenToSeeClinician: Women aged 30+ should visit their district health center for a quick, pain-free VIA screening examination.
ethiopiaContext: Nationwide school-based vaccination campaigns coordinated with regional health bureaus in Ethiopia.
